description: Presentations Attack at DEF CON 23 features offensive security talks covering penetration testing, network attacks, web application security, wireless exploits, and hardware hacking techniques (17 talks).

talks.title: NetRipper: Smart Traffic Sniffing for Penetration Testers
talks.teaser: NetRipper: Smart Traffic Sniffing for Penetration Testers
talks.summary:
The Challenge of Encrypted Network Traffic

Ionut Popescu introduces the challenge penetration testers face when intercepting network traffic on compromised hosts. When applications encrypt communication using TLS/SSL or proprietary protocols, external packet capture tools like Wireshark or tcpdump only capture unreadable ciphertext.

Architecture and Hooking Mechanism of NetRipper

NetRipper overcomes encryption by performing post-exploitation user-mode DLL injection into targeted processes. The tool hooks low-level socket and cryptographic API functions—such as send, WSASend, PR_Write, and SSL_write—capturing network payloads directly from memory before encryption occurs or immediately following decryption.

Configurable Filtering and Targeted Capture

To avoid overwhelming testers with massive traffic dumps, NetRipper implements intelligent in-memory filtering. Operators can configure regular expressions and string queries to capture only specific sensitive data, such as authentication credentials, session tokens, database connection strings, or administrative commands.

Practical Deployment Scenarios and Mitigations

Popescu demonstrates deploying NetRipper across popular applications, including web browsers, SSH clients, database management consoles, and thick-client enterprise software. Defending against user-mode hooking requires rigorous endpoint process monitoring, code signing enforcement, and host intrusion prevention systems.

talks.title: Abusing XSLT for Practical Attacks
talks.summary:
Understanding XSLT and the XML Processing Attack Surface

Fernando Arnaboldi of IOActive examines XML Stylesheet Language Transformations (XSLT), a Turing-complete language used by enterprise applications to convert XML documents into HTML, PDF, or alternative XML formats. Many developers overlook that untrusted XSLT stylesheets represent an expansive execution environment susceptible to severe exploitation.

Arbitrary File Disclosure and SSRF Vectors

Arnaboldi demonstrates how standard XSLT elements like document() can be abused to read local server files and perform Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) against internal network infrastructure. Attackers who can influence stylesheet inputs can exfiltrate sensitive system configurations and credentials.

Remote Code Execution via Native Extension Functions

The presentation details how vendor-specific extension mechanisms in popular XSLT engines (including Libxslt, Saxon, and Microsoft .NET XslCompiledTransform) permit arbitrary code execution. By embedding Java, C#, or external scripting calls directly within transformation templates, attackers can execute commands with the privileges of the web server.

Cryptographic Predictability in EXSLT Randomness

Beyond command execution, Arnaboldi reveals vulnerabilities in EXSLT random number generator implementations, showing that standard random() functions produce predictable pseudo-random output. Remediation requires disabling external entity resolution, restricting script extensions, and treating all XSLT templates as untrusted executable code.

(AI summary — Gemini 3.8 Flash)

talks.title: One Device to Pwn Them All
talks.teaser: One Device to Pwn Them All

talks.title: Hacker in the Wires
talks.summary:
The Concept of the Catchwire Inline Device

Dr. Phil Polstra introduces Catchwire, an open-source hardware implant designed to sit invisibly inline on physical Ethernet cabling. Unlike traditional network taps that require dual NICs or external monitoring stations, Catchwire functions as a transparent hardware drop box capable of deep packet inspection and attack execution.

Hardware Architecture and Transparent Bridging

The device is built around low-cost embedded Linux microcontrollers configured as transparent network bridges. Because it operates at Layer 2 without claiming an IP address on the target network, it remains completely undetectable to standard network mapping tools, intrusion detection systems, and network access control (NAC) mechanisms.

Command, Control, and Out-of-Band Communications

Catchwire establishes resilient out-of-band command channels using cellular modems, Bluetooth low energy, or hidden packet triggers embedded within normal network traffic. Polstra demonstrates how operators can send trigger packets that wake the device and initiate automated reconnaissance scripts.

Offensive Capabilities and Penetration Testing Use Cases

Polstra showcases practical exploitation scenarios, including sniffing plaintext credentials, injecting man-in-the-middle payloads, and executing automated network exploitation against unpatched internal servers like MS08-067. Mitigating inline hardware attacks requires physical security controls, IEEE 802.1X port authentication, and regular physical inspections of cable runs.

(AI summary — Gemini 3.8 Flash)

talks.title: Hacking Web Apps
talks.summary:
Moving Beyond Automated Vulnerability Scanning

Brent White criticizes the common industry practice of relying solely on automated vulnerability scanners during web application assessments. While scanners efficiently identify known static signatures, they fail to comprehend application context, business workflows, and complex authorization models.

The Power of Manual Application Mapping

White presents a thorough methodology for manual web application reconnaissance, mapping user roles, API endpoints, parameter structures, and client-side logic. By analyzing application traffic through intercepting proxies, penetration testers uncover subtle discrepancies that automated crawlers miss.

Exploiting Business Logic and Parameter Tampering

The presentation focuses on exploiting business logic flaws, race conditions, and parameter tampering in multi-step transactions. White demonstrates practical examples where altering hidden form fields, replaying state tokens, or manipulating numeric quantities allows attackers to bypass payment thresholds and escalate user privileges.

Delivering Context-Driven Security Reports

White concludes with guidance on transforming technical findings into actionable remediation guidance for software development teams. Effective penetration test reports illustrate complete exploit chains and business risk rather than providing isolated, uncontextualized scanner outputs.

(AI summary — Gemini 3.8 Flash)

talks.title: Dissecting the Design of SCADA Web HMIs: Hunting Vulns
talks.teaser: Dissecting the Design of SCADA Web HMIs: Hunting Vulns
talks.summary:
### Architecture of Modern SCADA Web HMIs
At 00:00 and 05:22, Aditya K. Sood examines how modern Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) and Industrial Control Systems (ICS) increasingly integrate web-based Human-Machine Interfaces (HMIs). Sood explains that web HMIs centralize monitoring and control for field devices such as PLCs and RTUs, but simultaneously transform traditional web application vulnerabilities into high-impact operational hazards for physical infrastructure.

### Remote File Inclusion and Arbitrary File Access
At 11:07, Sood explores directory traversal and unauthenticated Remote File Inclusion (RFI) flaws discovered across commercial SCADA web interfaces. He demonstrates how unsanitized parameter parsing allows remote attackers to read sensitive system configuration files, retrieve proprietary ladder logic scripts, and execute arbitrary code on the underlying controller hosts.

### Cross-Site Scripting and Operator Command Injection
At 17:50, the presentation investigates client-side attacks including Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) and Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF). Because web HMIs frequently maintain active administrative sessions for plant operators, an attacker can leverage stored XSS to impersonate operators, manipulate setpoints, and send unauthorized command packets directly to connected industrial machinery without physical access.

### Insecure Credential Storage and Zero-Day Disclosures
At 24:17 and 30:31, Sood showcases live exploit demonstrations and discusses vulnerabilities reported to ICS-CERT. He reveals common engineering anti-patterns, such as hardcoding supervisory passwords directly in client-side JavaScript configuration files and relying on unencrypted session tokens, leaving critical control surfaces trivial to hijack.

### Defense-in-Depth and ICS Hardening Strategies
Concluding between 35:41 and 36:29, Sood outlines essential defensive recommendations for industrial environments. He stresses rigorous input sanitization, strict air-gapping and network segmentation for HMI interfaces, multi-factor authentication, and collaborative vulnerability disclosure between security researchers and industrial vendors.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: How to Train Your RFID Hacking Tools
talks.teaser: How to Train Your RFID Hacking Tools
talks.summary:
Demystifying RFID and Access Control Architectures

Craig Young of Tripwire VERT explores the inner workings of Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) and Near Field Communication (NFC) technologies used in physical access control, transit cards, and asset tracking. The talk focuses on empowering security researchers to build custom automation and testing workflows around existing hardware tools.

Scripting the Proxmark3 Ecosystem

Young details programmatic interaction with the Proxmark3, the premier open-source tool for RFID research. By writing custom Lua scripts and interacting with the client command interface, researchers can automate tedious tag scanning, clone low-frequency (125 kHz) ProxCards, and execute dictionary attacks against high-frequency (13.56 MHz) Mifare Classic chips.

Tag Emulation and Reader Mode Interactions

The presentation demonstrates advanced tag emulation techniques, showing how portable hardware can simulate valid badges dynamically or act as rogue readers to harvest badge credentials from passersby. Young reviews the physical and electromagnetic nuances of antenna tuning and power transfer that dictate operational range.

Fuzzing Physical Access Readers and Mitigation Strategies

Beyond credential cloning, Young illustrates methods for fuzzing electronic door controllers by transmitting malformed badge IDs over the Wiegand protocol. Hardening physical access systems demands migrating away from unencrypted legacy RFID formats toward modern cryptographically authenticated credentials like DESFire EV2.

talks.title: Pivoting Without Rights: Introducing Pivoter
talks.summary:
The Challenge of Restricted Network Pivoting

Geoff Walton and Dave Kennedy discuss the hurdles penetration testers encounter when establishing network pivots from initial compromise footholds. Standard pivoting techniques often require root or local administrator privileges to install virtual network adapters, modify routing tables, or open raw sockets.

Architecture of the Pivoter Framework

The authors unveil Pivoter, an open-source tool designed specifically to enable seamless lateral movement and network tunneling from unprivileged user accounts. Operating entirely in user space, Pivoter establishes encrypted reverse tunnels back to the tester's command platform without triggering administrative alerts.

Proxy Chaining and Port Redirection Techniques

Pivoter implements dynamic SOCKS4a/5 proxies and transparent TCP port forwarding over standard outbound channels. The tool tunnels internal traffic seamlessly, allowing testers to run external scanning and exploitation tools like Nmap and Metasploit directly against isolated internal network enclaves.

Evasion and Enterprise Detection Engineering

Because Pivoter executes without administrative rights and blends its communication into permitted outbound protocols like SSH or HTTPS, traditional host-based intrusion prevention systems often miss it. Defending against unprivileged pivots requires comprehensive egress filtering, behavioral network monitoring, and endpoint process execution auditing.

(AI summary — Gemini 3.8 Flash)

talks.title: Scared Poopless – LTE and your laptop
talks.teaser: Scared Poopless – LTE and your laptop
talks.summary:
The Embedded Attack Surface of Cellular USB Modems

Mickey Shkatov and Jesse Michael investigate the attack surface of cellular LTE USB modems, dongles, and mobile hotspots commonly issued to corporate laptop users. These ubiquitous devices are typically perceived as simple peripheral radios, but internally they run full-featured embedded operating systems with extensive attack surfaces.

Firmware Architectures and Virtual Network Interfaces

The researchers reverse engineer several popular LTE dongles, revealing that they function as USB Ethernet adapters running embedded Linux or Android kernels with built-in web management portals, DHCP daemons, and DNS servers. Vulnerabilities in these onboard services directly expose host operating systems to local compromise.

Remote and Local Exploitation Chains

Shkatov and Michael demonstrate multiple practical exploit chains, including unauthenticated command injection via web administration APIs, cross-site scripting (XSS) triggering remote firmware flashing, and cellular network over-the-air (OTA) attacks. Compromising the modem enables attackers to execute man-in-the-middle attacks, DNS hijacking, and direct kernel exploitation on the attached computer.

Securing Mobile Endpoints Against Peripheral Threats

The presentation emphasizes that endpoint security models must treat cellular modems and peripheral USB network adapters as untrusted external networks. Organizations should enforce strict endpoint firewall rules on virtual interfaces, restrict USB device classes, and demand regular firmware patch updates from cellular hardware vendors.

(AI summary — Gemini 3.8 Flash)

talks.title: BurpKit: Using WebKit to Own the Web
talks.teaser: BurpKit: Using WebKit to Own the Web
talks.summary:
Limitations of Headless and Static Web Testing

Nadeem Douba addresses the shortcomings of traditional web application penetration testing tools when evaluating modern, single-page JavaScript applications. Standard proxy scanners struggle to evaluate complex DOM mutations, client-side event handlers, and asynchronous single-page application (SPA) state changes.

Integrating Headless WebKit into Burp Suite

Douba introduces BurpKit, an open-source extension that embeds a complete WebKit browser engine directly into PortSwigger's Burp Suite. By providing full DOM rendering, JavaScript execution, and bidirectional proxy communication, BurpKit allows security testers to inspect and manipulate rendered application state programmatically.

Automating DOM-Based Cross-Site Scripting Exploitation

BurpKit excels at detecting and exploiting client-side security flaws such as DOM-based Cross-Site Scripting (DOM XSS), client-side prototype manipulation, and open redirects. Testers can inject dynamic instrumentation scripts into the browser runtime to monitor JavaScript sinks, taint-trace sensitive variables, and verify exploitability in real time.

Extending Security Tooling with Scriptable Browser Contexts

The presentation showcases how developers and security researchers can leverage BurpKit's API to build custom automated workflows, perform authenticated screen captures, and simulate user interaction workflows. The extension bridges the gap between passive proxy analysis and dynamic client-side vulnerability assessment.

(AI summary — Gemini 3.8 Flash)

talks.title: Shall We Play a Game
talks.summary:
### Scripting Engines as Game Attack Surfaces
At 02:30 and 06:24, Tamas Szakaly investigates the security implications of embedding scripting engines—predominantly Lua and custom interpreters—inside commercial video game engines. While scripting languages accelerate gameplay development and modding support, developers frequently expose low-level native functions and fail to properly sandbox scripts executing untrusted multiplayer data.

### SMB Traversal and Remote DLL Loading via UNC Paths
At 12:57 and 19:58, Szakaly demonstrates how seemingly benign game scripting functions can be weaponized across local networks and multiplayer sessions. By feeding universal naming convention (UNC) file paths (`\\attacker\share\payload.dll`) into script-level file loaders, he forces the running game process to reach across the network and load arbitrary dynamic link libraries into memory.

### Unauthorized Memory Access and VM Sandbox Escapes
At 27:13 and 34:15, the presentation delves into Lua virtual machine internals and bytecode exploitation. Szakaly demonstrates how corrupting upvalue pointers (`upval` structures) within Lua closures allows attackers to break out of the scripting environment. By manipulating closure offsets in memory, an attacker gains arbitrary memory read and write primitives within the host game process.

### Mitigations for Game Developers and Mod Ecosystems
Concluding between 38:00 and 40:39, Szakaly outlines practical mitigations for game studios. He advises disabling dangerous Lua standard libraries (`io`, `os`, `package`), enforcing strict path validation to block UNC network paths, verifying bytecode integrity, and isolating mod execution within restricted privilege boundaries.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: I Hunt Penetration Testers: More Weaknesses in Tools and Procedures
talks.teaser: I Hunt Penetration Testers: More Weaknesses in Tools and Procedures
talks.summary:
Analyzing the Security Posture of Penetration Testing Tools

Dr. Wesley McGrew of Mississippi State University investigates a critical yet frequently neglected security concern: the vulnerabilities present in the tools, hardware, and operational procedures used by professional penetration testers. Attackers or monitored targets can exploit these weaknesses to turn the tables on testing teams.

Vulnerabilities in Wireless and Network Drop Boxes

McGrew examines widely deployed hardware drop boxes and tactical penetration testing devices, such as the Wi-Fi Pineapple and custom Raspberry Pi implants. He reveals vulnerabilities in their default configurations, unauthenticated administrative web consoles, and cleartext update mechanisms that allow targets to detect, hijack, or corrupt testing hardware.

Exploiting Metasploit and Framework Implementations

The presentation highlights software flaws and protocol weaknesses in popular exploitation frameworks, including Metasploit and automated scanning tools. McGrew demonstrates scenarios where malicious targets intentionally send crafted payloads, corrupt packet captures, or weaponized server responses back to the tester's scanning workstation, achieving remote code execution.

Operational Security Recommendations for Security Professionals

McGrew emphasizes that penetration testers must treat target environments as hostile, adversarial networks. Practitioners must harden testing laptops, enforce multi-factor authentication on field drop boxes, sandbox vulnerability scanners, and eliminate default credentials and unencrypted protocols from their operational toolsets.
